sections.title: Name and identification
sections.text: The current name is Gymnopus fusipes; Collybia fusipes is an older name still common in field guides. The cap is usually 3–7 cm across, convex at first and later more expanded, brown to reddish brown, often with darker blotches; it may become paler as it dries. The very widely spaced gills are white to pale buff and may develop rusty spots with age. The tough stem is pale near the cap, browner toward the base, deeply longitudinally grooved and spindle-shaped; its buried portion can continue into a dark pseudorhiza. There is no ring. The spore print is white; smell and taste are not distinctive.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: It grows in tufts at the base of, on the roots of, or on stumps of broadleaved trees, especially oaks and sometimes beeches. The stem base is often hidden in the soil and may need to be uncovered to see its spindle shape. Fruiting is mostly observed from summer into autumn, with the season varying by region. The fungus can be associated with root rot in oak.

sections.title: Similar species
sections.text: The combination of tufts at tree bases, very widely spaced gills, and a tough, grooved, spindle-shaped stem that is often buried is characteristic. Cap colour varies with moisture and age and is not enough to confirm the species. Examine complete specimens and their bases, as well as the habitat, rather than relying on a photograph or a single feature.

sections.title: Edibility and caution
sections.text: The DGfM lists Gymnopus fusipes among mushrooms associated with gastrointestinal syndrome. Some popular accounts mention historical or conditional food use, but views differ and the stem is very tough. As a precaution, do not eat it. A photograph or this entry cannot confirm the identity of a foraged specimen. After a suspected ingestion or symptoms, contact a poison centre or medical service promptly and keep the specimens or meal remains.

traits: Cap usually 3–7 cm, brown to reddish brown, sometimes dark-blotched and paling as it dries
Very widely spaced gills, white to pale buff, sometimes developing rusty spots with age
Tough stem 7–15 cm, pale near the cap and browner below, grooved, spindle-shaped and often buried; no ring
White spore print; smell and taste not distinctive
Tufted at the bases of broadleaved trees or on their roots and stumps, especially oak · summer to autumn
safetyNote: The DGfM lists Gymnopus fusipes among species associated with gastrointestinal syndrome. Despite older or conflicting mentions of food use, the cautious advice is not to eat it. Identification from a photograph alone is unreliable; contact a poison centre or medical service promptly after a suspected ingestion or symptoms.
